articles.title: Popular Kalyan bakery sealed after FDA finds wood-fired furnace
articles.summary: Trending News: A popular bakery in Kalyan has been sealed by food safety officials following a complaint over the use of a wood-fired furnace to bake bread.The actio.
articles.body: A popular bakery in Kalyan has been sealed by food safety officials following a complaint over the use of a wood-fired furnace to bake bread.The action was taken by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) against Prince Bakery in Thane's Kalyan district. Bakery employees said the department stepped in after receiving a complaint that the establishment was using a wood-burning furnace for its baking operations.The bakery makes bread in large quantities and supplies it to several shops across the city. With its products reaching a sizeable number of customers, the FDA's action has drawn attention to the way traditional bakeries continue to operate despite need for change.Officials sealed the premises during the inspection, while further proceedings by the department are expected to follow.Why wood-fired ovens are under scrutinyThe action comes against the backdrop of a Bombay High Court directive asking bakeries across Maharashtra to move away from coal- and wood-fired ovens.The court had directed bakeries to shift to cleaner alternatives, including LPG, piped gas and electric ovens, citing concerns over air pollution caused by the burning of coal and wood.For many traditional bakeries, though, making the switch isn't as simple as changing the fuel. Owners have argued that replacing old furnaces can be expensive, particularly when their ovens are built around traditional dome-shaped designs. Some have also maintained that changing the cooking method could affect the familiar taste and texture of their bread.But the court's position has been clear: businesses can't claim an unlimited right to continue practices that contribute to pollution when public health and the wider right to a clean environment are involved.The Kalyan bakery action is therefore another example of the authorities enforcing the push towards cleaner baking methods across Maharashtra.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Tomorrow's wars will demand combined strength  of all services & all domains: Navy chief at OTA passing-out parade
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: Emphasising the need for jointness between the tri-services, Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan on Sunday told newly-commissioned India.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Emphasising the need for jointness between the tri-services, Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan on Sunday told newly-commissioned Indian Army officers that “tomorrow’s wars will demand the combined strength of all Services and all domains”.The Navy chief was the reviewing officer of the passing out parade at the Indian Army Officers Training Academy (OTA) in Chennai.Quoting from the Rig Veda, the Admiral said, “Samano Mantrah’ - Our purpose is one. Irrespective of the colour of our uniforms, we must train together, operate together, and when called upon to do so, prevail together.”Addressing young Lieutenants who were formally commissioned into the Army after 11-month intense training, Admiral Swaminathan said, “Your mind is your biggest weapon. Technology can give you information, speed and precision, but it certainly cannot replace wisdom. Do not outsource your thinking to an algorithm.... Remember, there will be an occasion in your lives when a soldier will look towards you expectantly and ask: ‘What do we do now?’ At that moment, no textbook or power point presentation or Chat GPT will come to your rescue. That’s when your knowledge, awareness and study will win you the day.”He further said, “Understand technology. Know your adversary. Invest your time and energy in your subordinates. Never stop learning. Courage is a muscle. It strengthens every time you use it. Whether physical or moral, courage more often than not, means the ability to stand alone to your convictions. It cannot be downloaded in a crisis; it is built and ingrained over time, in the small choices we make every day.”The Navy chief told young Army officers, “There will be times when you have to tell your superior what he may not want to hear. There will be instances when taking responsibility is uncomfortable. But you need to muster the courage to do what is right, even when it is inconvenient. Because your troops may understand and forgive an honest mistake or accept a difficult decision. But they will never forget a leader who set the wrong example or abandoned them when they needed him or her the most.”Addressing foreign Army officers who graduated from the Academy, Admiral Swaminathan said, “To our friends from overseas: we are as proud of your achievements, as your own countries will be. You return home carrying the ethos of this Academy, and friendships forged through shared experiences, hardship and purpose. May you remain enduring bridges of friendship between our nations.”

articles.title: Board of Peace touts progress as Palestinians’ situation worsens
articles.summary: Humanitarian official Athena Rayburn dissects the Israeli tactics making life ‘untenable’ for millions of Palestinians.
articles.body:
In this episode, Athena Rayburn, the executive director of the Association of International Development Agencies, describes what daily life has become in the occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

In Gaza, more than two million Palestinians have been corralled into about 104sq km (40sq miles), where Israeli forces consistently bomb them. Basic human requirements like clean water, food, electricity, medicine and durable shelter are hard to come by, with Israel imposing severe restrictions on humanitarian aid and groups. The United States-backed Board of Peace touts progress, but Rayburn tells host Steve Clemons that the situation on the ground has become “untenable and catastrophic”.

articles.title: Aos 103 anos, morre idosa que viralizou nas redes sociais com vídeos de receitas de família | G1
articles.standfirst: Elma Andreani Alves conquistou mais de 6 milhões de visualizações com vídeos em que ensinava receitas como biscoito de polvilho, bolinho de batata com carne moída e pão recheado. A causa da morte não foi divulgada.
articles.summary: Elma Andreani Alves conquistou mais de 6 milhões de visualizações com vídeos em que ensinava receitas como biscoito de polvilho, bolinho de batata com carne moída e pão recheado. A causa da morte não foi divulgada.
articles.body:
Elma Andreani Alves, de 101 anos, viralizou nas redes sociais ensinando receitas de família — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

A idosa Elma Andreani Alves, de 103 anos, que conquistou mais de 6 milhões de visualizações nas redes sociais com vídeos em que ensinava receitas de família , morreu nesta segunda-feira (7), em São Paulo . O comunicado foi publicado nas redes sociais de Elma. A causa da morte não foi divulgada.

"Hoje, eu me despeço, com o coração profundamente apertado, da minha maior inspiração. Minha florzinha descansou, deixando em mim e em todos que tiveram a felicidade de conhecê-la um legado imenso de amor, carinho, doçura e alegria", escreveu a neta, Vivian Mezadri.

E ressaltou: "Ainda é difícil acreditar que não ouvirei sua voz, não verei seu sorriso e não sentirei sua presença como antes. Mas tudo continuará vivo nas minhas lembranças e no coração de cada pessoa que ela tocou [..] Chegou a hora da senhora descansar minha guerreira".

O g1 mostrou a história de Elma no dia 26 de julho de 2025, data em que se celebra o Dia dos Avós. Suas receitas, entre elas a de biscoito de polvilho, bolinho de batata com carne moída e pão recheado, ganharam o mundo pelas redes sociais. A ideia de fazer o perfil partiu da neta.

"Eu tinha 440 pessoas na minha rede social e atualizava um pouco porque trabalho com lembrancinhas. Mas um dia, eu estava sentada com a minha mãe no sofá, e minha avó sumiu. Perguntei: 'Mãe, cadê a avó?' Ela estava na cozinha. Aí falei que ia pegar o celular e filmar, porque estava fazendo o biscoito de polvilho. Eu a gravei cozinhando e tive a curiosidade de perguntar quantos anos ela tinha, para ela falar no vídeo a idade", relatou.

"Depois que gravei, falei: 'Depois eu posto'." Mas aí pensei de novo e disse para minha mãe: 'Quer saber? Vou postar'. Aí postei e no outro dia meu telefone estava daquele jeito, cheio de mensagens. Cada vez que atualizava eram mil visualizações. Aqueles comentários, um mais lindo do que o outro. É um prato afetivo. A gente ficou muito feliz."

A repercussão foi tão grande que virou rotina na casa: dona Elma passou a gravar receitas quase toda semana com Vivian e até acompanhava os comentários com entusiasmo. Um vídeo da receita do bolinho de batata com carne moída, por exemplo, alcançou 5 milhões de visualizações.

“Estou adorando. Foi muito bom para mim. A vida parece que melhorou mais. Estou querendo viver mais. Cada dia é melhor para mim. Estou muito feliz”, afirmou Elma ao g1, na época.

Elma Andreani Alves, de 101 anos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Natural de Uberlândia, Minas Gerais, dona Elma se mudou para São Paulo aos 15 anos. Ela se casou, teve quatro filhos e hoje tem 12 netos e seis bisnetos. Contou que aprendeu a cozinhar observando a mãe, ainda criança, e trabalhou por muitos anos em uma mercearia.

“Eu tinha sete anos quando minha mãe me dava um banquinho para subir e aprender a cozinhar. Ela costurava, e eu ficava ajudando. Desde pequena, fazia bolos para as vizinhas. Era bolo 'de nada,' bem simples, mas colocava canela e fazia”, lembrou.

"Antes de o meu marido falecer, a gente costumava fazer almoços para moradores de rua no Natal lá na casa que morávamos, no Jabaquara [Zona Sul da capital paulista]. Ele gostava de ajudar, e eu ficava dois dias cozinhando para o pessoal. Era uma delícia".

Elma ressaltou ao g1 que nunca usou um caderno de receitas. Tudo era feito de cabeça. Por isso, quando os vídeos viralizaram nas redes, a neta passou a medir os ingredientes com a avó para conseguir ensinar a receita para quem acompanha o perfil.

“Ela faz do jeitinho dela e depois eu que lute para ver quais são as medidas. Ela vê o ponto e não tem medida de nada. Não anota nada. Então, deixo-a fazer e depois vou medindo tudo. O interessante é que, se ela vê uma receita na Ana Maria Braga, pela TV, passa três dias e diz que vai fazer igual. E faz. Sem anotar nada. São impressionantes a lucidez e a memória dela”, contou a neta.

A fama repentina de Elma por conta dos vídeos nas redes sociais emocionou toda a família. Vivian ressaltou que sempre quis que a avó fosse reconhecida em vida.

E a avó não só entendia tudo como passou a falar a língua da internet, segundo a neta. " Ela é uma mulher guerreira que não parou no tempo e foi se atualizando. Ela sabe falar de tudo, qualquer assunto que você falar com ela, ela vai saber", ressaltou.

Segundo a neta, os vídeos não só reacenderam a vitalidade da avó como têm tocado os seguidores profundamente.

“Tem comentário de gente com depressão dizendo que se sentiu melhor vendo-a com essa sede de viver. Muitos falam que perderam as vovós ou as mães e que os vídeos ajudam. Além da comida, que une as pessoas, tem o afeto”, diz.

articles.body: NAGPUR: NCP (SP) MP Supriya Sule on Sunday signalled she would stop commenting on the ongoing discussion around the accident on Jan 28 near Baramati airport that claimed the life of her cousin, deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar, saying continued talk on the subject was creating misunderstandings among people.Sule said, "I will not speak on Ajit Pawar's accident going forward. There is continuous discussion on this issue, which is creating many misunderstandings. Therefore, with folded hands, my request is that I have stopped speaking on this topic from today." She did not elaborate further and declined to take additional questions on the matter.Enforce SC curbs across state, don’t be selectiveSule on Sunday said the state govt should implement Supreme Court’s 10pm cut-off for DJs uniformly across Maharashtra instead of imposing an outright ban in some cities and looking away elsewhere.On the controversy over playing DJs and loudspeakers, Sule said, “The matter has escalated. I would urge the govt to develop a consensus as there are big festivals like Ganeshotsav, Navratri and then Diwali. We need to sensibly bring all sections of society together and find a way forward.”Supporters of DJ have claimed students themselves are dancing in processions, “hence using them as a shield to impose a ban isn’t justified”. Sule drew a distinction. “There is no objection to dancing or to what anyone wants to do. The objection is about implementation. What does the Supreme Court’s order say? articles.title: Suspected drones near Amritsar airport trigger flight diversions, security alert
articles.summary: AMRITSAR: Suspected drone-like objects were reportedly spotted near Sri Guru Ram Das Ji International Airport late on Sunday night, triggering a major.
articles.body: AMRITSAR: Suspected drone-like objects were reportedly spotted near Sri Guru Ram Das Ji International Airport late on Sunday night, triggering a major security alert and leading to the diversion of seven incoming flights as a precautionary measure.Anirudh Sharma, who holds the additional charge of Airport Director, confirmed that drone-like objects were noticed in the vicinity of the airport. Following the alert, two incoming flights were diverted to Chandigarh and five to Delhi. Airport operations remained suspended from 9.50 pm to 11.15 pm, he said.Sources said the suspected flying objects were seen outside the airport's perimeter wall, following which Air Traffic Control (ATC) suspended landing operations due to concerns over the safety of aircraft operating in the area.Sources said the police suspect that the drones were flown locally.The incident is being viewed seriously, particularly because the international airport is located close to the India-Pakistan border. Security agencies were immediately alerted, while the matter was also reported to the police for investigation.Sources said the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), responsible for airport security, has also heightened its vigilance following the incidentWhile the exact nature and origin of the suspected objects are yet to be established, investigators are examining all possibilities. Sources did not rule out the possibility that locally operated drones may have entered the restricted airspace near the airport.However, given the increasing instances of drones allegedly being used from across the Pakistan border to smuggle narcotics, arms and ammunition into Punjab, security agencies are also examining whether there could be a cross-border angle, sources said.Sharma said the matter had been reported to the police, who are now investigating the incident to determine whether the suspicious flying objects were actually drones or some other objects and where they were flown from.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Amritsar | Silver Rate in Amritsar | Bank Holidays in Amritsar | Public Holidays in Amritsar | Petrol Price in Amritsar | Diesel Price in Amritsar | CNG Price in Amritsar | LPG Price in AmritsarStay updated with the latest Amritsar news. articles.title: A 69,000 sq ft data centre was planned beside Nashville Zoo; 600,000 people signed against it as a clouded leopard cub became the face of the fight to protect wildlife
articles.summary: US News: A proposed 69,000 sq ft data centre beside Nashville Zoo in Nashville, Tennessee, has triggered a huge public campaign, with nearly 600,000 people sig.
articles.body: A proposed 69,000 sq ft data centre beside Nashville Zoo in Nashville, Tennessee, has triggered a huge public campaign, with nearly 600,000 people signing a Change.org petition opposing the development. The project, proposed by digital infrastructure company DC BLOX, has raised concerns at the zoo over potential noise, artificial light and other impacts from round-the-clock data centre operations on vulnerable animals and conservation programmes. A young clouded leopard named Mayuree, born at the zoo in May 2026, became a powerful symbol of the campaign as the zoo urged supporters to oppose the project. The dispute has since moved beyond the petition, with Nashville officials introducing restrictions on large data centres and authorising steps that could allow the city to acquire the disputed property.Why Nashville Zoo opposed the data centreThe proposed development is located at 648 Grassmere Park, immediately adjacent to Nashville Zoo. The initial project application described a single-storey data centre of approximately 69,220 sq ft on a 23.49-acre property. The zoo raised concerns that a facility operating continuously could introduce persistent mechanical noise from cooling equipment and generators, along with artificial lighting and other infrastructure impacts. The zoo argued that such conditions could interfere with animal behaviour, biological rhythms and breeding programmes, particularly for species involved in conservation efforts. It has stressed that the issue is not simply the size of the proposed building but the potential cumulative effect of a large-scale, continuously operating industrial facility next to animal habitats.Nearly 600,000 people signed the petitionNashville Zoo launched its Change.org petition on June 3, 2026, calling on supporters to oppose the proposed development. The campaign quickly gained national attention, passing 400,000 signatures within days and continuing to grow throughout the summer. By late August, the zoo said nearly 600,000 people had signed the petition, while the Change.org page itself showed more than 599,000 verified signatures. The scale of the response turned what began as a local land-use dispute into a much larger public debate over the environmental and conservation implications of data centre development near sensitive facilities.Clouded leopard cub Mayuree became a symbol of the campaignMayuree was born at Nashville Zoo on May 5, 2026 and became the zoo's 51st clouded leopard born since 1991. The zoo participates in the Association of Zoos and Aquariums' Species Survival Plan for clouded leopards, making successful breeding an important part of its conservation work. Mayuree was also notable because she was the first clouded leopard cub at Nashville Zoo to be co-reared under the programme, combining maternal care with early human socialisation. As the zoo campaigned against the nearby development, photographs and updates about the young cub helped put a face on its concerns about protecting animals and maintaining successful conservation programmes.The zoo's concerns focused on noise and lightNashville Zoo has argued that the proposed data centre could create a very different sound and lighting environment from the one surrounding its existing animal habitats. Data centres require substantial cooling systems and backup power infrastructure, and the zoo has expressed particular concern about continuous operational noise, including sounds produced by cooling equipment and generators. It has also raised concerns about artificial lighting. The zoo's position is that vulnerable animals should not be exposed to potentially disruptive conditions without strong evidence that the impacts can be adequately controlled. Importantly, the zoo's concerns are about potential future impacts. There is no evidence that the proposed DC BLOX facility has already harmed Mayuree or other animals.DC BLOX disputed the concernsDC BLOX has defended its proposal and said the project can be designed to control the impacts highlighted by the zoo. The company said it planned to use closed-loop or waterless cooling and would comply with applicable noise and environmental requirements. It also said generators would be positioned away from the zoo and equipped with measures intended to reduce sound, including sound-attenuating enclosures and muffled exhaust systems. The company has argued that some claims about the project have been inaccurate or overstated and that appropriate engineering controls can address concerns about noise, lighting and other potential effects.The proposed development could be larger than the initial buildingThe 69,000 sq ft figure describes the building in the initial public permit application, but documents and subsequent reporting have raised questions about the longer-term development planned for the property. A geotechnical document reported by the Nashville Scene described a possible three-storey, 40-megawatt data centre along with a substation and associated infrastructure. Nashville Zoo has also said the wider plans could involve substantially more power capacity than the initial facility. These additional elements are important because the debate has focused not only on the footprint of the first building but also on what could ultimately be developed on the 23-acre site.Brad Paisley joined the campaignThe campaign also received support from country music star Brad Paisley, who publicly backed Nashville Zoo's opposition to the development and encouraged people to sign the petition. His involvement helped bring additional national attention to an issue that had initially centred on a proposed development in south Nashville. The combination of the zoo's conservation concerns, the rapidly growing petition and high-profile supporters helped make the project one of the city's most closely watched development disputes.Nashville imposed a temporary data centre moratoriumThe controversy eventually prompted direct action from Nashville officials. Mayor Freddie O'Connell issued an executive order directing city departments to examine the potential infrastructure, environmental and community impacts associated with large-scale data centres. Metro Council subsequently approved legislation establishing a temporary moratorium on the acceptance and processing of permits for data-centre developments. The council also adopted new zoning rules addressing data-centre uses and the conditions under which such facilities can operate. The measures reflect wider concerns around the infrastructure requirements of large data centres, including electricity demand, backup generators, fuel storage, cooling systems, substations, noise, lighting, stormwater and 24-hour operations.The disputed property became the centre of a bigger battleDC BLOX purchased the roughly 23.49-acre property for about $23 million in July 2026, adding another layer to the dispute. Rather than simply relying on zoning restrictions, Metro Nashville later approved legislation authorising the city to acquire the property through negotiation or condemnation for stated public purposes. Mayor O'Connell approved that legislation in August. The measure does not mean the city has already seized the property, but it gives Nashville a legal mechanism to pursue acquisition of the site.The data centre has not necessarily been stoppedDespite the petition, moratorium and potential acquisition of the property, the future of the project remains unresolved. The legal status of DC BLOX's proposal has become an important part of the dispute, with questions over whether the project could retain certain development rights because of actions taken before the city's new restrictions came into force. That means the nearly 600,000 petition signatures represent enormous public pressure but should not be described as having definitively cancelled the development. The fight has instead evolved into a broader legal and political dispute over land use, data-centre expansion and the protection of Nashville Zoo's conservation work.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: EBay's first full-time employee left the company after its IPO and built a $5.9 billion fortune; he has now donated about $1.2 billion into social-change projects
articles.summary: US News: Jeff Skoll, eBay's first full-time employee and president, played a crucial role in building the company before leaving after its 1998 public offering.
articles.body: Jeff Skoll, eBay's first full-time employee and president, played a crucial role in building the company before leaving after its 1998 public offering. He helped turn an online auction business into one of the defining technology companies of the internet boom, then chose a different path from the one usually associated with billionaires. Today, Forbes estimates his fortune at $5.9 billion, while his charitable Skoll Foundation and Skoll Global Threats Fund have donated about $1.2 billion worldwide over more than two decades. His journey has moved beyond technology, taking him into philanthropy, impact investing and filmmaking. From helping strangers trust one another in online transactions to funding people working on poverty, health and environmental problems, Skoll's story is ultimately about what happened after the fortune was made and what he decided it should be used for.How did eBay’s first full-time employee build a $5.9 billion fortuneJeff Skoll's path to extraordinary wealth began with a decision he initially doubted. According to Forbes, he met eBay founder Pierre Omidyar while studying for an MBA at Stanford University. When Omidyar approached him about the idea behind the online marketplace, Skoll was far from convinced before realising that Omidyar had spotted an important opportunity. Skoll joined the company during its early years and became its first full-time employee and president. According to ‘Celebrity Net Worth,’ he helped turn the young online auction site into a more organised business by writing its first business plan and developing its operational framework.He also helped establish the feedback system that allowed buyers and sellers to rate one another. At a time when online shopping was still unfamiliar to many people, this helped create trust between strangers carrying out transactions over the internet. The business grew rapidly. Celebrity Net Worth reports that eBay went public in September 1998, with its shares initially priced at $18 each. By April 1999, the company's market value had climbed to around $25 billion, making both Omidyar and Skoll billionaires.Leaving eBay marked the start of Jeff Skoll’s mission to drive social changeSkoll eventually stepped away from the company he had helped build. As per Forbes, he left eBay in 2001, three years after its IPO. His departure marked the beginning of a second career focused less on building personal wealth and more on addressing problems around the world. That shift was partly shaped by experiences much earlier in his life. According to Celebrity Net Worth, Skoll's father developed cancer when Skoll was a teenager and later expressed regret about not having enough time to pursue his dreams. The experience left a lasting impression on Skoll and influenced the way he thought about the purpose of work and wealth. The idea of ‘tikkun olam,’ a Jewish concept often translated as ‘to heal the world,’ also became an important part of his approach. Rather than simply treating his fortune as an end in itself, Skoll began to view it as a resource that could support people attempting to solve difficult social problems.How Jeff Skoll put billions into social-change projectsIn 1999, Skoll established the ‘Skoll Foundation,’ which supports people and organisations working on issues including poverty, education, public health and environmental challenges. Celebrity Net Worth reports that the foundation was an early supporter of social entrepreneurship, an approach centred on finding practical and innovative solutions to major problems. The scale of the effort has grown considerably over time. According to Forbes, the Skoll Foundation and the ‘Skoll Global Threats Fund’ have donated about $1.2 billion around the world during more than 20 years of work.The Skoll Foundation has organised the ‘Skoll World Forum’ since 2004. The gathering brings together people from business, government, philanthropy and civil society to discuss social change and the challenges facing communities worldwide. Skoll later expanded his philanthropic interests through the Skoll Global Threats Fund. As per Celebrity Net Worth, the fund focused on risks including climate change, water security, pandemics and nuclear proliferation. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Skoll personally donated more than $120 million to help provide medical equipment and testing supplies to underserved countries.Skoll expanded his efforts beyond philanthropy through impact investingGiving money away was not Skoll's only strategy. Celebrity Net Worth reports that he also became involved in impact investing through ‘Capricorn Investment Group’ and ‘The Rise Fund.’ The aim was to direct money towards businesses that could generate financial returns while also producing measurable social or environmental benefits. This reflected a broader belief that capital could be used in more than one way. Instead of separating philanthropy entirely from business, impact investing attempts to support companies whose work may contribute to improvements in areas such as healthcare, education or environmental sustainability. Skoll also publicly joined the ‘Giving Pledge,’ committing to give away the majority of his wealth during his lifetime.Skoll used filmmaking to raise awareness of major social issuesSkoll's interest in influencing society eventually took him to Hollywood. In 2004, he founded ‘Participant Media,’ a production company built around films and television projects intended to entertain audiences while drawing attention to important issues. Films associated with Participant Media include ‘An Inconvenient Truth,’ ‘The Help,’ ‘Lincoln,’ ‘Spotlight,’ ‘Roma’ and ‘American Factory.’ The company demonstrated Skoll's belief that storytelling could sometimes reach people in ways that reports, conferences and traditional campaigns could not.According to Forbes, Skoll announced in 2024 that Participant Media would close after two decades of operation. Today, Skoll's $5.9 billion fortune is a reminder of the wealth created during the rise of the internet. But the $1.2 billion donated by his charitable organisations tells that Skoll chose to spend much of the following decades trying to turn wealth, investment and storytelling into tools for wider social change.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Benjamin Choi, a 17-year-old who built a $300 mind-controlled prosthetic arm that reads brainwaves through non-invasive electrodes
articles.summary: US News: Each one of us spent the pandemic doing something that we normally wouldn't have the time to. While some picked up numerous indoor hobbies, others stu.
articles.body: Each one of us spent the pandemic doing something that we normally wouldn't have the time to. While some picked up numerous indoor hobbies, others studied hard enough to change career pathways. Benjamin Choi, a then 17-year-old kid, put his spare time during the phase to design an accessible device that does not require brain surgery.When he was in third grade, Choi watched a "60 Minutes" documentary about a mind-controlled prosthesis. Researchers implanted tiny sensors into the motor cortex of the brain of a patient who moved a robotic arm using her thoughts. “I was really, really amazed at the time because this technology was so impressive,” he said to Smithsonian Magazine. “But I was also alarmed that they require this really risky open brain surgery. And they're so inaccessible, costing in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.”Years later, when the pandemic hit in 2020, Choi, a tenth grader living in Virginia found himself with ample free time. The lab in which he’d planned to spend his summer researching aluminium fuels had shut down. But the documentary he had seen years earlier stuck with him, and he decided to use his spare time to build a less-invasive prosthetic arm himself.He formed a makeshift laboratory on the ping-pong table in his basement and designed the first version of his robotic arm using his sister's $75 3D printer and some fishing line. The printer couldn’t build pieces over 4.7 inches in length, so Choi printed the arm in tiny pieces and bolted and rubber-banded it together. In total, it took about 30 hours to print. This version worked using brain wave data and head gestures, and Choi posted instructions online for anyone to build their own.He had some previous experience building robots and coding from participating in competitive robotics at the elementary, middle school and high school levels, even going to the world championships several times. Starting in ninth grade, he taught himself the computer programming languages Python and C++ by watching videos on Stack Overflow, a website for programmers.After more than 75 design iterations, Choi's non-invasive, mind-controlled robotic arm could be made from engineering-grade materials, able to withstand weights up to about four tons. It operates using an algorithm driven by artificial intelligence (A.I.) that interprets a user’s brain waves. And it only costs around $300 to manufacture—a huge savings compared to what’s currently on the market. A more basic, body-powered upper limb prosthesis costs about $7,000. As of 2015, the very advanced, full-arm Modular Prosthetic Limb, which has 26 joints, hundreds of sensors and can curl up to 45 pounds, cost about $500,000. This prosthesis, paired with a surgery to reroute nerves that once controlled the arm, allows patients to command the limb with their thoughts and even feel texture through it.Choi’s arm uses electroencephalography, or EEG, to avoid the invasive techniques of other prostheses. EEG devices record the brain’s electrical activity using sensors placed on the head. They are often used in medicine to diagnose epilepsy or other brain disorders. His system uses two electrodes: a baseline sensor that clips onto the earlobe and another on the forehead that collects EEG data. The forehead electrode picks up brain wave information, which is sent to a microchip in the prosthetic arm via Bluetooth. An A.I. model that Choi created, also embedded in the chip, deciphers the data and converts it into a prediction of what the brain is thinking. The arm also moves using head gestures and stops with intentional blinks.The invention earned Choi a spot in the top 40 finalists of 2022's Regeneron Science Talent Search, America's oldest and most prestigious science and math competition for high school seniors. “It means a lot to me to see that my work is recognised like this,” Choi said at the time. “I'm definitely very grateful to be a finalist.” The young inventor went on to win funding from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2021 to continue his research and work with experts at the university. For about six months, he experimented with cloud computing to make the arm internet-compatible. To create his A.I. model, he worked independently with six adult volunteers for about two hours each, collecting their brain wave data at his school and home. While collecting the data via an electrode on the forehead, he asked each participant to focus on clenching and unclenching their hand. He trained the A.I. to distinguish between the brain signals, and the A.I. model continuously learns from a user’s brain waves. In total, the algorithm has over 23,000 lines of code, with 978 pages of math and seven completely new sub-algorithms. Choi’s algorithm performs with a mean accuracy of 95 per cent. He said the previous gold standard for a similar artificial neural network was 73.8 per cent.In 2021, he was selected as a Simons Fellow at Stony Brook University, where he worked remotely with Ji Liu, a professor in the department of electrical and computer engineering, on the machine learning algorithm of his AI. Choi has also won awards in the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair, the Microsoft Imagine Cup, and the National At-Home STEM Competition. He received a manufacturing grant in October 2020 from PolySpectra, Inc., a company that produces durable 3-D printed materials, to produce his arm.Over the past few years, Choi has only furthered his achievements. In 2023, he did machine learning research at The Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory. From August to December 2024, he worked as a researcher with NASA and currently works as an AI researcher at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He is about to graduate with a degree in applied math and a concurrent master's in computer science from the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences.The bionic arm, whose underlying signal processing he continued developing at Johns Hopkins, was the foundation of Choi’s interests. But his time at SEAS, whether with the Weber Group or Kempner Institute, has both broadened and refined his understanding of machine learning. Now set to enter the workforce, Choi is fully ready to continue what he’s always done: find ways to apply his research in the world around him.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: California turned a dirt lot beside Highway 41 into a $1.6M garden with 18 planting beds, murals, and space to grow food
articles.summary: US News: A former dirt lot situated near Freeway 41 and McKinley Avenue has got a new purpose, a greener one. The dirt lot, which sat neglected for years, was .
articles.body: A former dirt lot situated near Freeway 41 and McKinley Avenue has got a new purpose, a greener one. The dirt lot, which sat neglected for years, was transformed last week into a garden called the McKinley Peace Garden, where neighbours can grow tomatoes, herbs, or whatever (legal crops, of course) they choose, Fresnobee reported. The $1.6 million transformation was funded by the state's Caltrans agency, as part of the Clean CA Program, a $1.1 billion effort to enhance communities and clean up roadsides. On Friday, September 4, the garden was opened with a ribbon-cutting that drew local, state, and federal officials.Former dirt lot gets a colourful new lifeCaltrans worked with the city and several nonprofit organisations and decided to repurpose the vacant land that sits between the southbound Freeway 41 on-ramp and McKinley Avenue. Eighteen concrete planting beds now sit where dirt used to accumulate trash. An open-air, barn-style shelter provides shade. Two murals by artists Erica Thomas and Vanessa Gomez are featured on the iron fence that protects the garden. There's even a bathroom and storage, details that matter more than they sound when you're building something meant to last.“It’s taking advantage of an underutilised space within our community, turning it into something very, very beautiful, and that’s what we have here today, right here in the heart of our city,” Fresno Mayor Jerry Dyer said.He added that the project mirrors what the city has done with its Beautify Fresno campaign. “And that is to beautify spaces in our community, to restore curb appeal and to restore neighbourhood pride, and that’s what this garden will do.”Who gets to gardenFresno residents can use the garden. They can rent a plot for $41 annually, a fee that also covers water. That price point matters because it's accessible, but also signals that the garden isn’t free for all. The ones who care should invest. The city's Parks and Recreation Department will handle upkeep, and staff are already reaching out to households to spread the word. The city is working with Fresno Metro Ministry to contact residents within a one-mile radius of the garden to let them know about the project, Aaron A. Aguirre, Parks and Recreation Department director, said.You don’t necessarily have to be a seasoned gardener to rent a plot here. Even first-time gardening enthusiasts can try, as they provide free workshops, Dyer said.“I know there were people that had reservations about what this was going to look like and whether this was the right spot for this garden. But I think we can all say today, it was a good choice,” he said. In neighbourhoods where food access is fragmented and supermarkets are sparse, this community garden can really be a boon.The ribbon-cutting ceremony was also attended by Rep. Jim Costa, D-Fresno; Assemblymember Dr. Joaquin Arambula, D-Fresno; Michael Navarro, Caltrans District 6 director; Luis Martinez, representing Sen. Anna Caballero, D-Merced; and Councilmember Nelson Esparza.Nelson Esparza appreciated everyone involved in the development of the property, which he said had become somewhat of an eyesore. He pushed for the project and spent time searching for the right name. His mother eventually suggested ‘Peace Garden’, and that stuck. During the ceremony, he also thanked his mother, Brenda Hernandez, for helping him come up with a name for the garden. “What I love about community gardens is that they give people a reason to come outside, and more importantly, to give neighbours a chance to connect,” Esparza said.And just like that, the Peace Garden is open to Fresno residents. A lot that could have remained a dust trap for another decade is now a garden. The residents now have access to soil, sunlight, and the opportunity to grow something. This green space will shortly foster a community of people who deeply care about making a difference and transforming it into a green paradise. Are you a Fresno resident? articles.title: A farmer turned 70 acres of his Oregon barley farm into a wetland; now it hosts 140 bird species and endangered fish
articles.summary: US News: A farmer in southern Oregon transformed 70 acres of his 400-acre barley farm into a wetland in 2021, creating an unexpected refuge for wildlife while .
articles.body: A farmer in southern Oregon transformed 70 acres of his 400-acre barley farm into a wetland in 2021, creating an unexpected refuge for wildlife while helping address agricultural water pollution. Karl Wenner, a co-owner of Lakeside Farms near Klamath Falls, worked with conservation agencies and other partners to convert flood-prone farmland into a managed wetland. The area now attracts tens of thousands of ducks, geese and swans and supports at least 140 bird species, along with otters, beavers and muskrats. More significantly, the wetland has been used to raise federally endangered Lost River and shortnose suckers. In 2025, researchers found 50 adult-sized suckers after partially draining the wetland, offering a promising sign for species struggling with poor juvenile survival.Why an Oregon farmer turned 70 acres of his barley farm into a wetlandWenner became a co-owner of Lakeside Farms in 2017. The roughly 400-acre property had traditionally been used to grow barley and sits near Upper Klamath Lake, an important wetland and waterbird habitat in southern Oregon. Wenner initially appreciated the farm because its abundant water attracted ducks, but he later became concerned about the quality of water leaving the agricultural land. Tests showed that the water carried high concentrations of phosphorus, a nutrient that can contribute to harmful algal blooms in Upper Klamath Lake. Instead of continuing to farm the most flood-prone portion of the property, Wenner and his partners explored whether the land could be used to naturally filter agricultural runoff while providing wildlife habitat.The restoration project began taking shape in 2021, when about 70 acres of the farm were converted into a semi-permanent wetland. The area was engineered with shallow water areas, channels, dikes and islands that allow water to move slowly through the site. Rather than flowing directly towards Upper Klamath Lake, agricultural water can pass through the wetland, where vegetation and sediments capture nutrients and suspended material. The project was designed to provide environmental benefits without requiring the entire farm to be taken out of agricultural production. The remaining land continues to be used for farming, making the project an example of how restoration and agriculture can operate alongside each other.Wildlife responded quickly after the wetland was established. US Fish and Wildlife Service records documented more than 20,000 ducks using the property during October and November. Later reporting found that the restored area had attracted tens of thousands of ducks, geese and swans, while at least 140 bird species had been recorded at the farm. The wetland also became home to other wildlife, including otters, beavers and muskrats. Its rapid development into a productive habitat is particularly notable because the area had previously been used primarily as agricultural land.Plant diversity also increasedThe ecological changes were not limited to birds and mammals. Researchers used pollen collected by bees to study plant diversity around the farm. The analysis indicated that plant biodiversity had doubled within two years of the wetland restoration. Bee-based monitoring also helped identify native plants growing around the property and highlighted invasive species that could be targeted for removal. The approach gave researchers another way to measure how the landscape was changing as agricultural fields were replaced, at least partly, by wetland habitat.The wetland became a refuge for endangered fishThe project also took on significance for two endangered fish species found in the Klamath Basin. The Lost River sucker and shortnose sucker are both federally listed as endangered and are culturally important to the Klamath Tribes. Their populations have declined dramatically, with poor survival of young fish contributing to the difficulty of rebuilding their numbers. Conservationists therefore need places where juvenile suckers can survive and grow before eventually joining the wider lake population. Parts of the Lakeside Farms property were modified to provide such habitat, creating a protected environment that could serve as a nursery for the fish.Thousands of young suckers were introducedAs part of the conservation work, young suckers were introduced into ponds on the farm. Different releases and accounts have recorded varying numbers, with the broader project involving several thousand juvenile fish. The fish included endangered Lost River and shortnose suckers as well as native Klamath largescale suckers. The aim was not simply to increase the number of fish on the farm but to determine whether restored wetland conditions could allow young suckers to survive and develop in an environment resembling the shallow habitats that historically existed around Upper Klamath Lake.Researchers found 50 adult-sized fishA particularly significant development came in May 2025, when researchers partially drained the wetland to assess how the stocked fish had fared. They found 50 adult-sized suckers, with some measuring up to about 16 inches. The recovered fish appeared healthy and had reached a size comparable with mature fish. Researchers cautioned that the sampling might not have captured every fish in the wetland and that genetic testing was needed to determine the precise species composition of the recovered fish. The discovery nevertheless provided evidence that at least some stocked suckers had survived and grown substantially in the restored habitat.The discovery is important because the Klamath Basin's sucker populations face a serious recruitment problem. Many young fish fail to survive long enough to become adults, leaving existing populations dominated by older fish. Poor water quality, habitat loss, altered water flows and other environmental pressures have contributed to the decline. The Lakeside Farms project does not solve those wider problems, nor does the discovery of 50 adult-sized fish prove that a self-sustaining population has been established. It does, however, suggest that restored wetlands on working agricultural land could provide valuable rearing habitat for young suckers.The wetland also helps clean agricultural waterWildlife restoration was only part of the project's purpose. The wetland was also designed to improve the quality of water leaving the farm. Excess phosphorus entering Upper Klamath Lake can contribute to nutrient pollution and harmful algal blooms, which can create difficult conditions for aquatic life. By slowing water and allowing plants and sediments to absorb or retain nutrients, the wetland acts as a natural treatment system before water reaches the lake. Reports on the project indicate that phosphorus levels in water leaving the wetland were substantially reduced, demonstrating how agricultural land can potentially be used to address some of the environmental impacts associated with farming.A different model for farmland restorationThe project has attracted attention because the land has not simply been permanently removed from agriculture. Some fields can be managed as wetlands for periods before potentially returning to crop production. Flooding can also help suppress weeds and pests and may improve soil conditions. Wenner and his partners have therefore been testing whether farmers can receive ecological benefits while retaining an economically viable agricultural operation. Other landowners in the Klamath Basin have reportedly shown interest in similar approaches, suggesting that the experiment could eventually be replicated elsewhere.A project built on collaborationThe transformation was not carried out by Wenner alone. Lakeside Farms worked with federal and local conservation organisations, including the US Fish and Wildlife Service and Klamath Watershed Partnership. Funding and technical support helped with the wetland's design, construction and ongoing management. The project also brought agricultural interests into closer contact with conservation efforts involving the Klamath Tribes and endangered sucker recovery. That collaboration is significant in a region where disputes over water, farming and endangered species have persisted for decades.The wider Klamath Basin challengeThe significance of the farm becomes clearer when viewed against the history of the Klamath Basin. Large areas of the region's historic wetlands have been lost or altered, while agriculture has changed the way water moves through the landscape. Upper Klamath Lake remains an important habitat for migratory birds but also faces persistent water-quality challenges. The two endangered sucker species have suffered severe population declines, making the creation of additional shallow-water habitat particularly valuable. Against that backdrop, a 70-acre wetland may be relatively small, but it offers a practical demonstration of how individual farms can contribute to broader restoration efforts.A small farm experiment with a bigger possibilityThe Lakeside Farms project began with a relatively simple question about what to do with flood-prone farmland and polluted agricultural water. Four years after the wetland was created, the results had extended far beyond water treatment. Tens of thousands of waterfowl were using the property, at least 140 bird species had been recorded, plant diversity had increased and endangered suckers had survived to adult size. The project is not a complete solution to the Klamath Basin's environmental problems, but it demonstrates how a working farm can be redesigned to provide food, habitat and cleaner water at the same time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Delhi building collapse: 5 MCD officials suspended, death toll rises to 7 - key points
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The death toll in the Satya Niketan building collapse in southwest Delhi rose to 7 on Monday as rescue operations entered their second day,.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The death toll in the Satya Niketan building collapse in southwest Delhi rose to 7 on Monday as rescue operations entered their second day, while the Delhi government suspended five Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) officials over the tragedy.The probe further intensified with the owner of the building being apprehended in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, following a massive multi-state manhunt involving 10 police teams.Delhi Police had earlier issued a Look Out Circular (LOC) against him after he went untraceable following the collapse.The suspended officials include the MCD Deputy Commissioner, Executive Engineer, Superintending Engineer, Assistant Engineer and Junior Engineer. The action came as authorities faced questions over the safety of the decades-old building, which was being used as a boys' paying guest accommodation near Delhi University's South Campus.The multi-storey building collapsed at around 1.30 pm on Sunday while repair work was underway. Multiple agencies, including the Delhi Police, Delhi Fire Service, National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and Delhi Disaster Management Authority, continued rescue operations through the night. Death toll rises as rescue continuesSo far, 12 people have been pulled out of the debris, with seven reported dead earlier in the rescue operation. The search continued on Monday as teams worked through the remaining debris to determine whether anyone else was trapped.National Disaster Response Force Inspector General (IG) Narendra Bundela said the force did not have a "specific figure" on the number of people trapped under the debris.According to Bundela, the rescue operation involving the NDRF and agencies of the Delhi government was expected to continue until late Monday.The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) said 11 patients had been received at the JPN Apex Trauma Centre following the collapse."Out of the 11 patients, five were brought dead, while one patient who was in critical condition later succumbed to his injuries; three patients have been admitted and are being treated. One patient underwent limb surgery. One patient had sustained a minor injury and was discharged after observation," the statement read. Water, repair work under scannerDelhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta visited Satya Niketan on Monday to review the rescue operation. She said around 80% of the debris had been cleared, with teams focusing on the basement.Gupta said water accumulation in the basement, combined with repair work on the old structure, led to the collapse."Approximately 80 per cent of the debris has been cleared, with only the basement debris remaining. Water had accumulated in the basement, and the combination of this with ongoing repair work on the old structure led to the collapse," she said.The chief minister ordered the sealing of buildings in Delhi having a fifth floor and warned of action against officials found responsible."Strict action will be taken against MCD officials found responsible. Instructions have been issued to immediately seal buildings in Delhi having a fifth floor," she said in a statement.Gupta also said the building adjacent to the collapsed structure would be demolished after the debris was cleared, as it was considered extremely dangerous."Residents of the collapsed building and adjacent unsafe buildings have been evacuated. The standing building, which appears extremely dangerous, will be demolished once the debris is cleared," Gupta said. City-wide safety checks orderedThe Delhi government has ordered structural audits of similar buildings, with a policy being drafted to make owners of old buildings submit safety reports before operating PG accommodations, nursing homes, schools or other commercial establishments."A policy is also being drafted requiring owners of old buildings to submit structural audit reports and certify their safety before operating paying guest (PG) services, nursing homes, schools or other commercial establishments. Officials found responsible for negligence will also face immediate action," she said.The government had earlier ordered a magisterial inquiry and an FIR against the building owner following an on-site review."Following an on-site review and based on the preliminary assessment, the chief minister has ordered a magisterial inquiry into the incident and FIR against the building owner," the Delhi CMO had said in a post on X.Residents said many students staying in the area were from Keralam, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and studied at nearby colleges including Motilal Nehru College, Atma Ram Sanatan Dharm College and Sri Venkateswara College.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Nepal Police have warned people against keeping, selling or distributing valuables recovered from flood-hit areas, urging them to hand over such items to the authorities.In a statement issued on Sunday, police said using, concealing, buying or selling valuables found during the floods could constitute an offence and invite legal action.The police also cautioned that disasters can create conditions for increased theft, looting and fraud as security personnel remain engaged in search-and-rescue operations.The warning came days after 29 people were arrested in Dhading for allegedly breaking open a vault that had been swept downstream from Rasuwa and the upper catchment areas and taking cash from it.A joint patrol team of the Armed Police Force and Nepal Police reportedly caught the suspects at the site while they were allegedly extracting money from the damaged safe.In another case, Nepal Police arrested two men for allegedly stealing gold earrings from the body of a woman who was swept downstream by floods in the Narayani River. The incident came to light after a video of it went viral on social media.The police warning was not linked to any specific incident but came amid a series of reports of valuables being recovered from areas devastated by the floods.Flash floods triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.The Bhotekoshi River, flowing south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.The disaster has killed more than 1,300 people, while around 5,000 remain missing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Middle East News: Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town reportedly killed 11, including two children and two medics, on Monday morning.According to the state news.
articles.body: Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town reportedly killed 11, including two children and two medics, on Monday morning.According to the state news media, nine were killed in a post-midnight strike on a three-storey residential building, while the two paramedics died when the second strike hit a car.Israeli military claimed the attack was in retaliation for the drone attacks on its troops by the armed group Hezbollah in the occupied areas of Lebanon.According to Reuters, the airstrikes killed at least seven on Sunday, with Israel intensifying its bombardment of southern Lebanon despite a ceasefire brokered in June between Lebanese Hezbollah and the Israeli defence forces.The strikes on the town reportedly came without an online evacuation warning from the Israeli military.The Israeli military said it was looking into the reports, BBC reported.Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the attacks were a "dangerous escalation" that hampered the US-brokered ceasefire meant to end the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah.On March 2, Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel within days after Israel and the US struck Iran, after which Israel launched a massive air and ground offensive on Lebanon; 4,300 Lebanese citizens have died since then, with Israel occupying a major portion of the country’s southern half.Israeli military has continued striking both the occupied territories and the north, often reportedly without evacuation warnings.The IDF said it was looking into the reports regarding Monday strikes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 70-year-old Texas woman used $150,000 from her retirement savings to create an all-women tiny-home community spread across five acres for rent of $450 monthly
articles.summary: US News: Be it a divorce, a breakup, widowhood or single parenting, women are often left in situations where they have nowhere to go, no other home that they h.
articles.body: Be it a divorce, a breakup, widowhood or single parenting, women are often left in situations where they have nowhere to go, no other home that they have invested in and no other residence whose doors are open for them. This is why Robyn Yerian, a 70-year-old Texas woman spent about $150,000 from her retirement savings to build an all-women tiny-home community. Eleven residents now live there and rely on each other for company and practical help, according to a report by inkl.com.Called the Bird's Nest, the community is located on five acres in Cumby, a small town roughly an hour northeast of Dallas. She opened it in 2022, drawing money from her 401(k) retirement account after working out that her savings alone would not carry her through retirement.A single empty-nester, she said the idea grew out of her worry about the rising cost of living around Dallas. Robyn herself first moved into a tiny two-bed in 2016 after watching the TV show, Tiny Home Nation, a documentary about people living in mini-homes. Later, she decided a second plot could bring in more passive income. "I just took a leap of faith," she told People, describing the choice to sink her savings into land and construction.The site has concrete pads with rent starting from $450 a month, close to half the going rate in Cumby. Residents pay that to park a recreational vehicle or set down their own tiny home. The gated community only has two rules: no men and no drama. Moreover, residents enjoy an idyllic life with access to fire pits, yoga sessions, book clubs and a private pool. The demand for her pads has far outrun the supply, with more than 500 women on the waiting list for a place. "This community is our little utopia," said Robyn to Metro UK. "We have dogs running around, and get together all the time. We are a bunch of really great friends."It takes a woman to build a villageYerian did not begin with the intention of only housing women. "It's all women. It just kind of evolved that way," she said in a CBS Texas interview. At first, Robyn advertised The Bird’s Nest to anyone aged over 55, but after hosting a workshop for a group of women, teaching them how to use power tools, she pivoted to the idea of a women-only commune.She pointed out that most people living in tiny homes on a fixed income are retired women, a group she knew would be hunting for cheaper ways to live. Robyn said she "didn’t want to exclude men", but that this was "all about empowering women."Getting the site off the ground was the harder part. Tiny homes are barred from many areas, so Yerian looked for unincorporated land outside Dallas, then had the plot zoned as an RV park. "Getting zoned was the hardest part," she told Realtor.com.The residents at Bird's Nest are aged between 60 and 80 and mostly single, divorced or widowed. They gather at an outdoor pavilion they call the kitchen and have a unique rule: grievances are aired directly and put to rest. "I won’t put up with drama, pettiness, talking behind people’s backs – we don’t do that here. If we have an issue, we will say something."There’s a process for welcoming new members, too, as Robyn will initially speak to interested parties over the phone before inviting them to Texas to spend a few days on the land, with each plot coming with its own deck and a garden with flowers and landscaping. "I spend a lot of time vetting people," Robyn explained, adding that she’s after a "caring person who wants to be part of a real community."Beyond just housingFor residents of the community, the appeal of the place extends beyond just low-rent housing. "It is literally a sisterhood," resident Donna Welborn told the broadcaster, saying she had not expected the group to grow so close.The group also helps out when someone falls ill. Cheryl Huff came through heart surgery earlier in the year with her neighbours around her. "There's somebody there that's gonna help you out," she said, describing a group that shares meals, lifts, and errands.The Bird's Nest has drawn national attention at a time when many women retire with less than men. According to a Goldman Sachs report, 28% of retired American women have less than $50,000 (£36,700) saved.Affordable, sociable housing for older women remains scarce, and Yerian has said she will not lift the $450 (£330) rent. She has cast the project as women supporting women, and urged others to build something like it.Now, Robyn said she would "never change" her way of life and is glad to have introduced others to her alternative way of living. "Everyone in the community now is from all over the state. They came, met us, and decided they wanted to be here – sold their home and bought a tiny home," she concluded. "This is our final home; we won’t be going back. We hope to keep each other’s company for as long as we can."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Malcolm X: "You don't have to be a man to fight for freedom. All you have to do is…" - why standing up for freedom belongs to everyone
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Malcolm X's words push back directly against the idea that fighting for freedom is somehow reserved for a particular kind of person. \"You don't have t.
articles.body: Malcolm X's words push back directly against the idea that fighting for freedom is somehow reserved for a particular kind of person. "You don't have to be a man to fight for freedom," he said. "All you have to do is to be an intelligent human being." This line is attributed to a speech he delivered at the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem, the venue where he regularly held meetings for the Organization of Afro-American Unity, the group he founded in 1964 after leaving the Nation of Islam. Malcolm X spent much of his life speaking directly to ordinary people rather than only to other activists or leaders, and this particular quote captures something genuinely central to his message, that the capacity to recognise injustice and resist it does not belong to any single group of people. It belongs to anyone genuinely willing to look clearly at the world around them.Quote of the day by Malcolm X"You don't have to be a man to fight for freedom. All you have to do is to be an intelligent human being"What did Malcolm X actually mean by this quoteThe quote draws a real distinction between two very different qualifications for standing up against injustice. One is a kind of physical or social status, being a "man" in the narrower, traditional sense the word often carried. The other is simply the willingness to think clearly and honestly about what is actually happening around you. Malcolm X is arguing that the second quality matters considerably more than the first. Fighting for freedom, in his framing, was never really about physical strength or formal authority. It was about genuinely understanding your own situation well enough to recognise when something is wrong, and having the will to actually do something about it.Why intelligence, in this sense, means something broader than educationWhen Malcolm X speaks of being an "intelligent human being," he is not necessarily talking about formal schooling or academic achievement. He is describing something closer to clear-eyed awareness, the ability to genuinely see a situation for what it actually is, rather than accepting an explanation simply because it is convenient or familiar. Malcolm X himself famously educated himself extensively while in prison, reading widely and building his own understanding of history and politics largely outside any formal institution. That personal history gives this particular kind of "intelligence" a genuinely practical meaning. It is less about credentials and more about the discipline to actually think for yourself.Why this quote reaches well beyond its original contextAlthough Malcolm X was speaking specifically about the civil rights struggle of his own era, the underlying idea reaches considerably further than that one particular moment. Throughout history, meaningful resistance to injustice has rarely come only from people with an obvious claim to power or authority. It has very often come from ordinary people who simply refused to accept an unfair situation once they had actually understood it clearly. The quote suggests that anyone capable of genuinely recognising injustice already holds the real qualification needed to stand against it, regardless of their background, position or status.Why clarity of thought matters so much in the face of injusticeInjustice often survives specifically because people are discouraged from thinking clearly about it. A situation can be presented as normal, inevitable, or simply too complicated to actually challenge. Malcolm X's emphasis on intelligence points directly at this problem. Genuinely understanding a situation, rather than simply accepting the explanation given for it, is very often the first real step toward actually changing it. That is precisely why education, reading and independent thought featured so heavily in his own personal transformation, and why he consistently encouraged others to develop the same habits for themselves.Why the quote challenges a narrow idea of who gets to leadBy explicitly saying you do not have to be a "man" to fight for freedom, Malcolm X was directly rejecting a genuinely narrow, exclusionary idea of who was actually qualified to resist injustice. That framing opens the fight for freedom to absolutely anyone willing to engage with it honestly, regardless of gender, age or standing. The real qualification, in his words, was simply the willingness to think clearly and act on what you actually understood to be true.Other memorable quotes by Malcolm X"A man who stands for nothing will fall for anything.""Education is the passport to the future, for tomorrow belongs to those who prepare for it today.""You can't separate peace from freedom because no one can be at peace unless he has his freedom.""If you're not ready to die for it, put the word 'freedom' out of your vocabulary."How to apply this quote by Malcolm X in daily lifeMalcolm X's message can genuinely apply well beyond any specific historical movement. It suggests that recognising an unfair situation, whether at work, in a community or in wider society, does not require any special status or authority. It simply requires paying real attention and thinking honestly about what is actually happening. Reading widely, questioning an explanation that feels too convenient, and staying genuinely curious about the world around you are all ways of building exactly the kind of intelligence Malcolm X was describing. Standing up against something unfair does not have to wait for permission or position. It simply requires the willingness to see clearly and act on what you actually see.Why this quote still resonates todayThe idea that anyone can recognise injustice and act against it remains genuinely relevant, since the temptation to assume that meaningful change is someone else's responsibility never really goes away. Malcolm X's words are a reminder that the real barrier to standing up for what is right was rarely ever a lack of status or authority. It was, and still is, a lack of clear, honest thinking about what is actually happening. Anyone willing to genuinely look at their own situation and think it through carefully already holds the one qualification that actually matters.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Timothy Armoo, who started a tutoring business at 14, sold a company for eight figures at 27 and is now putting $6.7 million of his own money into young AI founders
articles.summary: UK News: Timothy Armoo was thinking like an entrepreneur at 14. By his late 20s he had built and sold a company for eight figures. Now the British entrepreneur.
articles.body: Timothy Armoo was thinking like an entrepreneur at 14. By his late 20s he had built and sold a company for eight figures. Now the British entrepreneur is not only investing his fortune but backing a new generation of founders betting on artificial intelligence with millions of his own money reports Fortune. The Legon Fund, founded by Armoo, will have a £5 million ($6.7 million) investment pot to back minority-led AI startups. The move is a reflection of his belief that AI is the next big opportunity for young people to build wealth and businesses. Armoo’s journey into entrepreneurship began far removed from the traditional startup world. He lived with his grandmother in Ghana during his early years before relocating to London. His family later lived on a council estate in a landscape spoiled by gang violence and knife crime, adds the report. Armoo began his first company at 14 years old with limited financial resources, and no network of business contacts. His tutoring business grew to 65 tutors in six weeks. At 17, he had already closed his first business acquisition deal, selling his publication Entrepreneur Express to Horizon Media and later his entrepreneurial ambitions continued even at university.From university project to $10 million+ exitIn 2017, Armoo founded Fanbytes, an influencer marketing agency, in his second year at university. It took advantage of the growing importance of social media marketing, winning major clients such as the U.K. government, Deliveroo and Samsung. Five years later, Brainlabs acquired Fanbytes for eight figures. At the time Armoo was just 27 years old, thus making him a millionaire before the age of 30. His experience with social media shaped his views on how technology can open up new opportunities. He now views AI as the next big shift in technology that could lower the barriers to entrepreneurship.Why Armoo sees AI as a game changer"Aspiring entrepreneurs have tools at their disposal that previous generations could never have imagined," Armoo said in a statment to Fortune. Artificial intelligence can assist people in brainstorming, prototyping and doing work that used to need dedicated teams. This allows social platforms to then offer distribution and access to potential customers without traditional advertising budgets. For young founders, it means that it’s possible to start a business from your laptop with relatively little money up front. The other reason Armoo thinks AI could be a huge wealth-creation opportunity is accessibility.$6.7 million to support young foundersThe Legon Fund is Armoo’s way of putting that belief into action. He’s contributed some $6.7M of his own fortune to fund AI startups founded by minority entrepreneurs. The fund seeks to solve one of the problems that can prevent promising ideas from becoming viable companies: access to capital. Armoo’s own experience has shaped the approach. The tech that helped create his wealth was social media, but he believes AI now offers a similar opportunity.The entrepreneurs of tomorrowArmoo’s gamble comes as young workers are facing a tough job market for entry-level jobs. The traditional corporate path is less sure as AI adoption and slower hiring take hold, and many Gen Z workers are becoming more interested in entrepreneurship. Founder is among the fastest-growing job titles Gen Z is pursuing, according to data shared by Fortune from LinkedIn. And Intuit’s Entrepreneurship in 2026 report found that 43% of Gen Z respondents were considering starting a business in 2026, the highest share among age groups. The transition has been made easier by digital infrastructure. Websites, social media, video conferencing, online payments and AI tools mean that entrepreneurs can launch and market businesses without the physical infrastructure that used to be required.From entrepreneur to supporterNow Armoo’s story has taken a different path. He is no longer just creating businesses on his own. With the Legon Fund, he’s looking to give young founders the capital to build businesses out of AI-driven ideas. Whether or not AI will turn out to be the wealth-creation wave Armoo anticipates is yet to be seen. But the millions of his own money he’s willing to commit show how seriously he takes the opportunity — and how determined he is to make sure other young entrepreneurs can take part.Images Courtesy: istock and FortuneCatch the latest World News and Live updates.
