articles.title: Inside Charlie Kirk’s effort to develop the next generation of conservative voices
articles.summary: Charlie Kirk's closest colleagues reveal how the TPUSA founder mentored Gen Z conservatives individually, shaping media voices and activist careers.
articles.body: When Charlie Kirk was assassinated at 31, he left behind an organization that had helped young conservatives find their voices and, for some, launch careers in media and activism. One year later, those who worked closely with him say they are carrying forward the model he built, continuing to recruit and mentor college students and young activists. "I don't think anybody can replace Charlie," Turning Point USA chief of staff Michael McCoy, who also worked as Kirk's chief of staff, told Fox News Digital. "I think there's a massive void that was left behind in his absence." Kirk was shot and killed while holding an event at Utah Valley University. The TPUSA founder and CEO was known for his "Prove Me Wrong" events, during which he would invite people to debate him and ask questions. His Sept. 10, 2025, event where he was murdered was part of his "American Comeback Tour." CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION: TIMELINE OF UTAH CAMPUS SHOOTING, TYLER ROBINSON CHARGED Prior to Kirk's assassination, TPUSA had 410 college chapters registered for the 2025-2026 school year. After Kirk was murdered, that number grew to 1,095. The organization also saw its Club America chapters, aimed at high schoolers, grow substantially. Before Sept. 10, 2025, there were 454 Club America chapters, and after Kirk's assassination, the number grew to 3,102. The growth in the organization exemplified one of Kirk's main goals, which was to develop young conservative voices. "The Charlie Kirk Show" executive producer Andrew Kolvet remembered Kirk as being "intentional" when building a bench of activists. "He wanted to use that as sort of like the farm system for voices that could find their footing, find their way, and really, the cream would rise to the top," Kolvet told Fox News Digital. Kolvet pointed to Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt as examples of Turning Point alumni who went on to hold high-profile public roles. ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION Isabel Brown, a former Turning Point USA staffer who now hosts "The Isabel Brown Show" at The Daily Wire, said Kirk helped steer her from a planned career as a trauma surgeon toward activism and conservative media. Brown first encountered Turning Point as a college student and later helped Kirk plan an event at Colorado State University, her alma mater, an experience that cemented her interest in the work. "I was having so much darn fun planning this event and many others that we would go on to put on for our campus that Charlie said, ‘I don't think you're meant to work in a fluorescently lit hospital for the rest of your life. I think you are supposed to do something a little bit different,’" Brown recalled. Brown went on to work for TPUSA, becoming one of the young conservative media voices shaped by Kirk’s organization. Brown's experiences with Kirk in the early days of TPUSA reflected his approach to young conservatives, according to those who worked with him. Rather than simply looking to build an audience for the sake of having one, they said, Kirk sought out students individually and encouraged those in whom he saw potential. "He was not just trying to gain a whole swath of numbers of college students or build this 30,000-foot-scale army that could take on the political machine," Brown said. "He was interested in the individual student sitting in front of him, and he was that way until the day that he died." BENNY JOHNSON RECALLS HOW CHARLIE KIRK HELPED HIS FAMILY AFTER ARSON DESTROYED THEIR DC HOME Kolvet said Kirk's ability to connect with young conservatives came from his willingness to engage with them without trying to imitate aspects of culture that didn't speak to him. "What made Charlie different when it came to reaching young people was that he just rejected all of the pop culture stuff. He never pandered to them," Kolvet said. "He was just himself." Blake Neff, a producer on "The Charlie Kirk Show," said Kirk's influence online was rooted in his interactions with people in real life. "Charlie very much lived in the real world. He was a social media celebrity, but he was not a social-media inhabitant. He was not obsessed constantly with what was getting what was getting views," Neff said, adding that to Kirk the social media success was "almost a side effect of the work he did." Neff noted that Kirk not only went to college campuses across the country, but also was engaged in local and national politics. The TPUSA CEO and founder would also frequently travel to meet voters, donors and "different Americans in different walks of life," according to Neff. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE McCoy said Kirk's success reaching Gen Z stemmed from his "authenticity and consistency." "Gen Z has this ability to kind of sniff out who's being authentic and who's not, and we really aren't a generation that likes to be pandered to," McCoy, a Gen Zer, said to Fox News Digital. "We don't like it when people show up to try to speak the lingo or kind of participate in the culture of Gen Z because we can kind of see right through that. But Charlie, he showed up with a message that he knew young people ought to hear, not that we wanted to hear oftentimes, and he was rewarded for it." For McCoy, Kirk's influence can be seen not only through the personalities that have emerged from TPUSA, but also in the students who seek to model their activism after Kirk's. "Charlie was kind of the head figure for so many of our students at Turning Point USA because they saw him, and they copied him by going on college campuses and kind of doing a micro version of what he was doing, talking to students, tabling, handing out stickers and buttons and rally signs and talking about conservative principles," McCoy said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kolvet said that students have told him that they try to emulate Kirk's courage and willingness to face any audience, including hostile ones. "He was so bold. He was a lion for the Christian faith. He held nothing back. He didn't mince words. He didn't cower. He would go full bore right into the fray. He would [go] right into places where, you know, we were most not wanted," Kolvet told Fox News Digital. "He was willing to be exactly who he was and speak truth in any context."

articles.title: 18 years ago, US govt took over finance giants Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac: Why it mattered amid 2008 crisis
articles.summary: News News: Eighteen years ago on September 7, 2008, the US government made a public announcement about a sweeping intervention to rescue Fannie Mae and Freddie M.
articles.body: Eighteen years ago on September 7, 2008, the US government made a public announcement about a sweeping intervention to rescue Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, two mortgage-finance giants whose troubles had become a threat to the country's housing market and wider financial system.The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) and the US Treasury publicly announced that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac had been placed under government conservatorship. The companies had formally entered conservatorship a day earlier, on September 6, with the consent of their boards.The intervention came as the US housing market was collapsing and mortgage defaults were mounting, setting the stage for the global financial crisis.Why the takeover matteredAs the housing downturn deepened, losses mounted at Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, raising concerns about their ability to meet their financial obligations and continue supporting the mortgage market.The stakes were high. Allowing either company to fail could have disrupted a major source of mortgage financing, unsettled investors holding their debt and mortgage-backed securities, and added further pressure to an already weakening housing market.The government therefore stepped in to prevent the two companies' financial problems from becoming a broader shock. On September 6, 2008, FHFA placed both into conservatorship, taking control of their management, boards and shareholders. The companies, however, continued operating as corporations.The Treasury also agreed to provide financial support, effectively creating a government backstop that allowed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to continue meeting their obligations and supporting the mortgage market.The intervention helped contain the immediate threat posed by the two mortgage giants, but it did not end the financial crisis. Just eight days later, Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, intensifying turmoil across global financial markets.Thus, ultimately, what was initially viewed as an emergency measure has lasted nearly two decades.Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain under federal conservatorship in 2026. FHFA continues to oversee them, while Treasury provides financial support under agreements first signed on September 7, 2008.The Treasury has since invested heavily in the companies. According to a Yale case study, the two firms ultimately received a combined $191.5 billion in Treasury investments between 2008 and 2017.In January 2025, Treasury and FHFA amended their agreements to address the eventual release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from conservatorship, but the companies have yet to leave government control.Even president Donald Trump has revived the possibility of taking the two mortgage giants public, although there is no confirmed timeline for an offering.Trump had tried to end government control of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during his first term.Then, in June, after appointing FHFA Director Bill Pulte as acting director of national intelligence, Trump was asked whether Pulte's new role meant an IPO was off the table.“No, it’s not. We’re thinking about an IPO for that. It’s not a rush,” Trump said, adding that Pulte would remain at FHFA.The potential move comes with significant challenges. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain deeply embedded in the US mortgage market, buying mortgages from lenders and packaging or guaranteeing them for investors. Experts have warned that removing the government backstop without a carefully structured replacement could increase risk for mortgage-backed securities investors and ultimately push up borrowing costs for homebuyers.How housing crisis became a financial crisisThe US had experienced a major housing boom in the years before 2008, fuelled by expanding mortgage credit and rising property prices. Thus, when house prices began falling, borrowers increasingly struggled to repay their mortgages, while lenders and investors faced mounting losses.The Federal Reserve later described the end of the US housing boom and the rise in subprime mortgage delinquencies as the proximate cause of the financial crisis. Problems in the wider financial system, including excessive leverage and underestimation of credit risks, amplified the shock.At the centre of the US mortgage market were Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, two government-sponsored enterprises that bought mortgages from lenders and guaranteed or packaged them into mortgage-backed securities. Their role helped lenders replenish funds and maintain the flow of mortgage credit to homebuyers.By the time of the intervention, the two companies together held or guaranteed about $5.2 trillion in home mortgage debt, according to research published by the American Economic Association. Their securities were also widely held by banks, investors and financial institutions around the world.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Will Trump succeed in restarting Russia-Ukraine peace talks?
articles.summary: The Witkoff-Kushner visit to Moscow and Kyiv did not produce a breakthrough, but it can help begin a new process.
articles.body:
The visit by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv has left more questions than answers. Details of what was discussed in both meetings are scant, but all participants seem to describe them as “positive”.

It is indeed a positive development that US President Donald Trump is trying to jump start negotiations at this point. The biggest problem he faces is that Russia’s position has only hardened.

Russia wants Ukraine to be genuinely neutral, with no Western military presence, open or clandestine. It wants to keep previously occupied territories and it insists that Ukraine withdraw from the small part of Donbas that remains in its hands.

Moscow demands a cap on the size of the Ukrainian army and on the types of weapons it may possess. It also wants far-right units and paramilitary groups disbanded and outlawed, the legislation limiting the use of the Russian language cancelled and elections to be held in which Russia-friendly parties could compete freely with the pro-Western ones.

For Ukraine and its European backers, this would be a hard pill to swallow, all the more so after spending the summer trying to convince the European public and Trump that the “tide is turning” in the war.

As evidence, Ukrainian and Western officials have repeatedly pointed to the Russian offensive slowing down and Ukraine intensifying strikes deep within Russian territory, targeting oil facilities and causing fuel shortages across the country.

The campaign against Russian energy infrastructure was meant to coerce Russian President Vladimir Putin into accepting peace on conditions more favourable to Ukraine.

But the opposite has happened. Russia’s negotiating position is now even less open to compromise. The land swap, once eyed as a way to compensate Ukraine for its withdrawal from the Donbas region, is now out of the question.

Meanwhile, the Kremlin has launched its own devastating campaign of strikes aimed at collapsing Ukraine’s economy. In addition to shutting down exports of Ukraine’s main commodities, grain and ore, through Odesa ports, Russia is also methodically destroying logistical hubs and warehouses owned by large retailers as well as large-scale industry, from metallurgical plants to beverage factories.

This is the point when Trump’s peacemaking duo resurfaced on the Russo-Ukrainian front after a protracted absence. The very fact that Kushner and Witkoff embarked on this trip and were received by Putin personally signals a change of tack in Washington.

A week before their arrival, CIA director John Ratcliffe mysteriously appeared in Moscow. Ratcliffe was effectively snubbed by Putin, who refused an audience when the CIA chief’s convoy reached the Kremlin. Instead, Ratcliffe had meetings with the heads of Russian security agencies, FSB and SVR, before heading home.

Nothing emerged from this meeting, apart from media speculation based on dubious sourcing. Hawkish media outlets claimed that Ratcliffe arrived with a stern warning against Russia attacking East European NATO members.

Others claimed Ratcliffe was trying to convey the “tide is turning” narrative to Putin and push for new negotiations based on that. The Atlantic magazine claimed last month that it was the CIA director who planted the idea that Russia was beginning to lose into Trump’s head during golf games.

Russian emigre outlet Agentstvo confirmed , quoting a Kremlin source, that Putin cancelled the meeting after hearing what Ratcliffe had been telling his subordinates and concluding that he was delusional.

Whether that is true or not, it is quite telling that Ratcliffe, who is a more senior US official than Kushner and Witkoff, was turned away, while they received a warm welcome in Moscow and spent a considerable time with Putin. Clearly, Trump’s envoys did not make the long trip to repeat what the Russian president sees as Western propaganda.

Whether Kushner and Witkoff’s mission has added anything substantial to the peace process is another question. They expressed cautious optimism regarding their progress. They said that no immediate breakthrough was foreseen but were eyeing direct trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US.

What is remarkable about the Witkoff-Kushner mission is the sheer number of commentators who were all too keen to claim that it was doomed from the outset. This is a reflection of the power pro-war circles continue to wield, despite growing war fatigue in Western societies.

The pro-war party simply wants any talks with Russia to be doomed, like they wanted the Istanbul talks to be doomed in the spring of 2022 and Minsk agreements to be ditched before that.

In trying to jump-start the peace talks, Trump will also have to face off with this party, which includes, European governments, NATO leadership and parts of the political establishment in his own country.

He would be keen to achieve some progress in peace talks prior to midterm elections and pressure Putin into limiting his military cooperation with Iran, but that’s impossible to achieve while the US plays a crucial role in helping Ukraine target infrastructure in Russia’s own territory.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s resilience is increasingly under question amid continuing brutal bombardment by the Russian army. As winter approaches, the targeting of energy and water infrastructure could severely worsen living conditions in the country.

Kyiv is already shaken by a political crisis, aggravated by corruption scandals involving top officials close to Zelenskyy, as well as a turf war between security agencies. There is also a $26bn gap in the Ukrainian defence budget, which needs to be covered by Western aid that’s not necessarily forthcoming.

There is no limit to warmongers pressuring Ukraine into fighting a suicidal war with a far stronger rival, but there is a limit to how long Ukrainians would be willing to die for an agenda that’s increasingly at odds with their national and personal interests.

articles.summary: Argentina’s sovereignty claim is enshrined in its constitution, but oil production raises the economic stakes.
articles.body:
A dispute between Argentina and Britain over control of the Falkland Islands has flared up again, after Argentinian President Javier Milei said the “winds of change” favour his country’s claim to the self-governing overseas United Kingdom territory.

Argentina’s presidency said in a statement on Friday that it had ordered the opening of proceedings to “investigate and penalise” 45 entities “linked to the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons” around the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.

The remarks followed comments from US President Donald Trump that the United States was reviewing its position on the Falkland Islands. Washington has threatened to oppose Britain’s sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago if it does not increase its NATO defence spending.

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting responded by asserting Britain’s “unshakeable” commitment to the Falklands. “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” he said in a social media post.

Residents of the Falkland Islands have indicated they prefer to remain a part of the UK, and British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the country would “resolutely uphold” their right to self-determination.

Why do the Falkland Islands matter to the UK and Argentina?

Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, located about 600km (375 miles) east of Argentina’s southernmost tip.

It ended with the surrender of Argentine troops after 74 days of fighting that killed 649 Argentines and 255 British troops.

Argentina’s sovereignty claim is enshrined in its constitution and is frequently invoked as an expression of national identity. Milei said the islands are “our future” and that Argentina needs to “recover” them as a matter of national importance.

The right-wing libertarian is preparing to seek re-election in October 2027 as his approval ratings plummet. Polls show only around 34 percent of Argentines support his drastic belt-tightening and deregulation policies.

Plans for large-scale oil production around the islands raise the economic stakes of the dispute. Milei declared that the Sea Lion deep-sea oil project, a joint UK-Israel operation, was a “clear and present danger” to the country’s claims.

Production at the field about 220km (140 miles) north of the islands is expected to begin in 2028. Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own. “Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security,” Milei said.

Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum brushed off Milei’s threats in a joint statement on Friday, saying they would press ahead with the Sea Lion plan under licences granted by the Falkland Islands government and backed by Britain.

The United States has signalled it may change its long-held position on the future of the Falklands. For decades, successive US administrations have remained neutral on the competing claims while recognising Britain’s de facto administration of the islands.

A departure from that position risks inflaming already high transatlantic tensions between Washington and its NATO allies.

Milei said the US was considering a change in position because it sees Argentina as a “reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come”.

The Argentinian leader is a regular feature at conservative pro-Trump political gatherings in the US, and Trump has previously described the far-right populist leader as his “favourite president”.

Trump has repeatedly criticised Britain over its stance on the US-Israel war on Iran, accusing it of not assisting Washington in the fight against Tehran and of failing to help the US reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Benjamin Gedan, director of the Latin America programme at the Stimson Center in Washington, DC, said hints of a change to US neutrality in the dispute over the Falklands were clearly designed to needle British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Despite the good relationship between Trump and Milei, any resolution of the Falklands dispute still depends on persuading the UK. “Any settlement of this long-standing dispute will surely involve negotiations,” Gedan said. “And that means persuading the British, not the Americans.”

articles.title: ‘That’s a dog kennel’: London Tube’s ‘calm space’ in station met with public ridicule and confusion
articles.summary: A pilot project trialing a “calm space” for neurodivergent subway travelers in London has been met with bemusement — and some gentle ridicule — from the public, due to the size, design and location of the new refuge.
articles.body: A pilot project trialing a “calm space” for neurodivergent subway travelers in London has been met with bemusement — and some gentle ridicule — from the public, due to the size, design and location of the new refuge. The initiative by subway and bus authority Transport for London (TFL) aims to support neurodivergent travelers — including the more than one in 100 people in the UK on the autism spectrum, many of whom face intense sensory challenges from loud noises and crowded spaces. In the trial, a small, open-fronted pod manufactured by US firm NOOK has been placed at Ealing Broadway Tube station in west London. The idea is to “support customers who may find travelling overwhelming and need a quiet space to pause, regulate and recover before continuing their journey,” TFL said in a statement published Friday. The trial is being run in partnership with autism charity Autistica, it said. TFL also posted about the Ealing Broadway trial on Facebook, where many users praised the aim of the initiative — but questioned its execution. “From someone that needs it…It doesn’t look like a calm space to me (the construction nor the location),” wrote one Facebook user. “But appreciate the thought.” Others questioned the size of the space, with multiple comments likening it to a “dog kennel.” “It looks like a calm space for ants,” wrote one commenter. Another criticized the choice of location. “If it’s supposed to be a ‘calm’ place, then it’s at the wrong location at the top of the stairs to the platforms and near the lifts,” she wrote. Another commenter offered constructive criticism about the design. “As someone who’s autistic, that needs a door,” she wrote. “You’re literally exposed, it’s just a bench with a roof,” she added. “Good effort but maybe turn it the other way so people won’t be like animals in a zoo and gawped at.” Other comments included one claiming that “the calm space is basically a cupboard;” another that questioned whether it was designed for the diminutive Hobbit people from J.R.R. Tolkien’s fantasy books; and one person who said they could “just picture teenagers in there vaping or a drunk person asleep!” The pod will remain in place for at least four weeks, said TFL, which added that another calm space will be trialed at the London Transport Museum in Covent Garden for a period of eight weeks. CNN has reached out to TFL for further comment. Autistica offered a statement from its senior research manager, Michelle Newman, stressing the importance of accessible transport. “As we push for neuroinclusive spaces in education, healthcare, and employment, we’re reminded that accessibility must start with the journey to these places,” she said.

images.caption: One Facebook commenter described the refuge as "a calm space for ants."

articles.title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
articles.summary: The new leadership is trying to maintain both confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits.
articles.body:
The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.

It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR).

In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away.

Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience.

The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes.

So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it.

In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors.

The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos.

"Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely.

It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence?

The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years.

"Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th".

OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock ?

This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable.

"The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said.

Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget.

Chancellor refuses to rule out tax hikes in October Budget

UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget

There was a focus on growth. As he toured the MTC, a centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, he said the UK's "great talent and latent potential" made it the third most innovative country in the world, and he wanted to translate that into economic growth and success in more areas.

Two decades ago, Healey was responsible for the Regional Development Agencies, scrapped by the Coalition Government, that helped fund this very facility.

In his speech there was a big clue about how to square the circle of investing in industrial policy at a time of tricky public finances.

The "Pufins" - public finance institutions - such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund can invest strategically, less constrained by the government's borrowing rules. Part of the plan is Pufins to breed more unicorns ($1bn tech startups) in the UK.

This is the other part of the global backdrop. Amid the tumult of trade and military wars, there is arguably one of the biggest financial events in world history.

In the coming weeks, hundreds of billions of dollars will be invested and trillions in value confirmed from flotations of big American AI firms. The UK has some standout technology in this sector. The government wants to promote it.

The chancellor was also, however, cautious about the impact of AI on security and on jobs. Some degree of "public control" could be required to make these changes work for everyone. It appeared a little less cheerleading than the stance of the Starmer administration.

The chancellor was perhaps mindful of the army of manufacturing robots, laser welders, 3D metal printers, whirring into action around him.

Long term, it will be growth that will determine whether his borrowing rules are met, he said.

Ultimately he will be judged by his actual policy choices, but where there are trade-offs between balancing the books and economic growth across the country, this sounds like a chancellor who might prioritise the latter.

articles.title: German far-right party candidate thanks Musk after state election win
articles.summary: A German far-right political party’s candidate singled out tech billionaire Elon Musk after a state election victory on Sunday. “Thank you, @elonmusk, for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time — including here in Germany,” Ulrich Siegmund, of the Alternative for Germany party, or AfD,…
articles.body:
A German far-right political party’s candidate singled out tech billionaire Elon Musk after a state election victory on Sunday.

“Thank you, @elonmusk, for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time — including here in Germany,” Ulrich Siegmund, of the Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, wrote Sunday on the social platform X .

Siegmund’s post was made in response to Musk writing “Gut gemacht,” which translates to “good job” in English.

The AfD won the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, a German state, in a landslide but fell just short of a majority, according to The Associated Press. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz later said his center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party was “deeply shocked” by “the most serious election defeat that the CDU has had for years, for decades.”

President Trump on Sunday had posted an image to his Truth Social platform showing the AfD’s improved polling over the years.

Musk has long been supportive of the antimigration and Russia-friendly party. During a virtual appearance at a rally for the AfD in January 2025, the Tesla and SpaceX founder said he viewed the party as the “best hope for Germany,” urging German voters to “move beyond” the “past guilt” of older generations in a reference to the country’s Nazi past.

The tech mogul’s comments came after Musk wrote an op-ed for a German news outlet expressing his support for the AfD.

After Germany’s government labeled the party as an “extremist” political group in some regions of the country earlier last year, both Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio blasted the move . Rubio described it as “tyranny in disguise” in a May 2025 social media post.

Days later, Republican Sen. Tom Cotton (Ark.) asked then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to refrain from sharing intelligence with the German domestic intelligence agency until the AfD was treated as a “legitimate opposition party” and not as a “right-wing extremist organization.”

The AfD has rejected any accusations of being undemocratic or even anticonstitutional, the AP reported .

articles.title: Meet Callum Smith: The 23-year-old armless racing driver who steers with his feet at 110mph, joins Team BRIT alongside quadruple amputee Harvey Phillips and targets a historic Le Mans debut
articles.summary: UK News: Callum Smith has never let the absence of arms stand between him and his passion for motorsport. The 23-year-old from Nuneaton, Warwickshire, was born.
articles.body: Callum Smith has never let the absence of arms stand between him and his passion for motorsport. The 23-year-old from Nuneaton, Warwickshire, was born without arms but is now chasing an extraordinary dream, becoming the first armless racing driver to compete at the legendary 24 Hours of Le Mans.Smith, a finance assistant, has signed his first driver contract with Team BRIT, described as the world's only competitive racing team made up entirely of disabled drivers. He is currently training in the team's modified BMW 1 Series at Donington Park as he works towards obtaining his racing licence.From watching bike racing with his grandad to driving at more than 110mphSmith's love for motorsport began when he was just two years old. He would watch bike racing with his grandfather, Michael Smith, who was a major influence on his early interest in racing.His first track day came in July 2025 at Donington Park, where he reached a top speed of 90mph around the iconic 2.5-mile circuit. By April this year, he had pushed his speed further, recording 100mph on Silverstone's 3.66-mile Grand Prix circuit while driving his own Audi A3.He has since taken the next step by getting behind the wheel of Team BRIT's specially modified BMW 1 Series, where he has already reached speeds of more than 110mph.Speaking to SWNS, Smith said he always believed he had what it took to become a racing driver."Once I started getting into driving, I always had that self belief that I had what it took to be a racing driver and knew that I could do it."He added that Team BRIT had given him the opportunity to demonstrate his ability and pursue a dream that once seemed difficult to imagine.How Callum Smith steers a race car using his feetSmith drives using a specially designed steering plate created by Jim Doran Hand Controls. The system allows him to control the car using his feet.His left foot is used to steer, while his right foot operates the accelerator and brake. Additional controls have also been adapted to allow him to operate other functions inside the vehicle."On top of the accelerator I have an indicator switch – I have a Lodgesons Bleeper System which gives me buttons for the horn, main beam, window wipers etc.," he explained.Describing the steering system, Smith said, "I steer with my left foot. It's a steering wheel in the footwell that operates the steering wheel."'My feet are like my hands'Smith was born without arms because of an unexplained bilateral upper-limb disability. However, he says he has never regarded his disability as something that should prevent him from doing the things he enjoys."My feet are like my hands," he said, explaining that he writes with his right foot, plays video games such as FIFA and Call of Duty using his feet, and even plays the guitar that way.He also eats independently using a regular knife and fork.His approach to everyday life has helped him adapt naturally to driving, although racing presents its own set of challenges.A bold email to Team BRIT started his racing journeySmith's opportunity with Team BRIT began with an email in which he asked whether the team would be willing to help make his racing ambitions a reality."The racing started off with an email to Team BRIT expressing my interest in racing and I said if they were interested in making my dreams come true, I'd be forever grateful," he recalled.The team responded, and Smith went through tests with instructors before completing a skid test. From there, his journey towards becoming a competitive racing driver began.He is now working towards securing his full racing licence. One of the challenges he has to overcome is demonstrating that he can independently undo his harness and open the car door.'There's a lot of eye-to-foot coordination'While Smith is confident behind the wheel, he admits that adapting to a race car has been challenging."It's hard, there's a lot of eye to foot coordination," he said.One of the biggest surprises for him has been the physical demands of racing, particularly the weight and stiffness of the steering."The biggest surprise to me is how heavy the steering feels in a race car, everything is stiffer," he said.Despite that, Smith remains determined to continue."But I love it and I'm quite keen to get it sorted, I'm motivated to get it done," he said, adding: "Confidence I'm not short of, but it's going to be a lot of hard work."Quadruple amputee Harvey Phillips also joins Team BRITSmith is not the only new driver hoping to make history with Team BRIT. The team's latest driver line-up also includes 21-year-old quadruple amputee Harvey Phillips from Louth, Lincolnshire.Phillips lost parts of both legs, his right arm up to the elbow, as well as fingers and thumbs on his left hand after suffering meningitis when he was nine months old.He has developed his own way of controlling the car. A lever allows him to accelerate and brake, while a 3D-printed cup attached to his right arm helps him steer."To accelerate and brake I have a lever, I twist it down to accelerate and push it down towards the dash to brake," Phillips explained.He added, "I have a 3D printed cup to slot my right arm into to turn the steering wheel."Team BRIT has its sights set on the 24 Hours of Le MansFor Phillips, the immediate goal is to become comfortable with the race car and establish a competitive race pace."Getting comfortable with the car and getting a race pace down are the main aims for me," he said.But the team's ambition extends far beyond individual racing licences and track days. Team BRIT ultimately wants to become the first team comprising entirely disabled drivers to compete in the 24 Hours of Le Mans, one of the world's most prestigious endurance races.Both Smith and Phillips are now seeking sponsors as they embark on a year-long training programme. For Smith in particular, the journey represents the chance to break new ground in motorsport, and prove that the absence of arms does not have to mean the end of a racing dream.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Man 'planned paint protest at Johnson wedding party'
articles.summary: A court hears Tim Speers, from Cornwall, planned to write the word "Palestine" on the venue's lawn.
articles.body:
An alleged activist planned to spray the word "Palestine" on a lawn at Boris Johnson's wedding party venue, a court has heard.

Jurors at Southwark Crown Court were told police approached Tim Speers, 41, at a Cotswold estate as they thought he looked "quite out of place". The former prime minister was due to celebrate his marriage to Carrie Johnson at the Gloucestershire site the following day.

During the opening of Speers' trial, the jury was told police found Speers and another man - who is due to face trial at a later date - were carrying spray paint and super glue.

Speers, of Fairfield Road in Bude, Cornwall, denies having items with intent to damage property. The trial continues.

Jurors were told Speers and the man were stopped with cans of beers at the Daylesford Estate - which belongs to Conservative Party donor Lord Anthony Bamford - on 29 July 2022.

They initially refused to tell police why they were there and then said they were on holiday, the jury heard.

Prosecutor Christiaan Moll told the court a voice note recorded by Speers the day before his arrest was found by police, in which he said he had been asked by two people from Palestine Action to take part in "action", which he had "agreed to do".

Jurors were told Speers said in the voice message: "There's this big heart mowed into his lawn, so the idea is to just go up to it and write Palestine in red paint, through a weed sprayer."

Moll said the voice note added: "So basically that Lord Bamford is hosting some like party this weekend, Boris Johnson.

"Lord Bamford is like the owner, his family the owner of JCB if no-one's aware… the Israeli government basically use JCBs to bulldoze Palestinian homes to create way for Israeli settlers, so this dude just profits from untold suffering."

The prosecution said Speers was expected to accept he had the paint and glue, as well as making the voice note, but would likely say he had abandoned the planned protest after arriving at the estate and noticing the large security presence.

The Johnsons were married in a private ceremony at Westminster Cathedral in May 2021. They hosted their wedding celebrations at Daylesford House on 30 July the following year, setting up marquees and hay bales in the grounds.

articles.title: Erika Kirk reflects on first year of grief after Charlie Kirk's assassination in NYT essay
articles.summary: Erika Kirk reveals the advice Usha Vance gave her after Charlie Kirk's assassination that became her lifeline through a year of unimaginable grief.
articles.body: Erika Kirk explained why simply getting "through the next 15 minutes" has been a critical step in getting through the first year since the tragic assassination of her husband Charlie Kirk. Kirk, who took over leadership of Turning Point USA (TPUSA) following the fatal shooting of her 31-year-old husband at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, penned a New York Times guest essay headlined, "What I’ve learned about grief," that was published on Monday. Kirk said the first 24 hours after her husband was assassinated felt "like a fever dream," and she told second lady Usha Vance that she didn’t know how she would move forward. The wife of Vice President JD Vance then offered words that are now "seared into" Kirk’s heart. JD VANCE'S WIFE USHA DETAILS HOW CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH INFLUENCED DECISION TO HAVE FOURTH CHILD "You know when you’re on an airplane with your kids, and you’re going to land in 15 minutes, but the kids are going crazy, screaming, throwing things, and then the plane lands, and the kids relax, and everything is fine again? That’s how it will be. Just get through the next 15 minutes," Vance told Kirk, according to Kirk’s guest essay. Kirk explained that things like seeing his toothbrush and towel in their shared bathroom were tough, but she constantly thought of Vance’s advice. "I stood in the doorway of our bedroom. I turned on the light and walked toward his side of the bed. I stared at his pillow and wondered how long a person’s scent can last in sheets. I stood there in silence, replaying all of the completely ordinary mornings we woke up there together. I wasn’t ready to be there, so I turned off the light and crawled into bed with my 3-year-old daughter. Just get through the next 15 minutes," Kirk wrote. "For months, I avoided my bedroom. I told myself it was OK to confront the pain gradually and to sit with each memory as it came to me," she continued. "The first Saturday without a love note from him passed. His 32nd birthday. My birthday. Thanksgiving. When I put the Christmas tree together wrong, it made me realize that being a widow means old traditions will need to make room for new ones. The wave crashes on me again and again. Every time, just get through the next 15 minutes." The CEO of the conservative nonprofit listed other family milestones that her beloved late husband had missed, and she eventually realized their young daughter was also "surviving her own little crashing waves." "Grief is strange. Time continues even when every part of you wants it to pause or, better yet, rewind. But the people we love who have passed on would not want us to spend the rest of our lives trying to rewind. At first, I needed to survive the next 15 minutes. Over time, I’ve realized that Charlie would want me to live them," Kirk wrote. "Occasionally, I’m asked whether I’m angry at God. I say no. My husband was one of one. I was blessed to be his wife, and I understood his assignment here on Earth, which he more than fulfilled. He wanted people who felt lost to know the everlasting hope he found through faith and the sense of meaning and purpose that can fill the deeper longings we so often try to satisfy elsewhere," she added. "To the world, he was Charlie Kirk. But to me, he was the love of my life. To our children, he was the center of their world." Kirk believes that it’s easy to struggle to understand God’s plan after losing a loved one and faith is truly tested when "bad things happen." HOW CHARLIE KIRK INSPIRED HIS MENTOR'S FIGHT TO DEFEND REALITY "True faith means accepting that we won’t get every answer and finding peace in that," Kirk wrote. "I have seen extraordinary good born out of something unimaginably evil. I have watched people return to faith in droves, reconcile with their families and forgive old wounds because of Charlie. I know my husband is in heaven, but I ache for him to be here. Still, I can stand and say without a shadow of a doubt that God is good." She wrote that the wave still comes, but it is different a year later, and she even welcomes it, as "a moment the grief makes Charlie feel impossibly close." Kirk believes grief is universal," doesn’t care whom you voted for" and never truly goes away. "I am learning that grieving Charlie and living life at the same time are part of the rhythm of grief. I can miss him with every part of me and still laugh with our children. I can have a broken heart and still experience joy," Kirk wrote. "If you are living through grief, I won’t tell you what to feel or that tomorrow will be better than today. I will tell you what a dear friend told me: Just get through the next 15 minutes," she continued. "One day, maybe when you least expect it, you’ll start to see that those 15 minutes hold more than just grief. The grief is there, always, but so is the beautiful gift of life." CHARLIE KIRK'S FAMILY COMES FACE TO FACE WITH ACCUSED ASSASSIN FOR FIRST TIME Psychotherapist and author Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital that the second lady provided strong advice. "One of the hardest parts of grief is that your mind races ahead, filling you with anxiety. How am I going to do this for the next year? How am I going to raise my kids without this person? What are holidays going to look like? How do I build a life I never expected to be living? Suddenly you’re trying to solve the rest of your life at the worst possible moment.Sometimes you really do need to shrink the window and just get through the next 15 minutes," Alpert said. "Resilience isn’t pretending you’re fine. It’s being able to hurt and still live your life," he added. "Erika’s piece shows that those two things can exist at the same time." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP TPUSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Charlie Kirk founded TPUSA to promote conservatism on college campuses nationwide. He was speaking before more than 2,000 people at a TPUSA event in Orem, Utah, where he was assassinated, leaving behind Erika and their two children. Fox News Digital’s Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.

articles.title: A Dublin teenager spent about €500 making a sea-salt hair spray for a school project; 6 years later his brand has grown into a €200,000 business
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Gavin Hefferon was a transition year student at St Andrew's College in Dublin in 2019 when he created a sea salt spray as part of a school business pr.
articles.body: Gavin Hefferon was a transition year student at St Andrew's College in Dublin in 2019 when he created a sea salt spray as part of a school business project, inspired by the wind-blown hairstyles worn by surfers. The initial investment was around €500, which covered basic packaging costs. Six years later, that same spray remains the best-selling product in his company's range. Hefferon left UCD, where he had been studying sustainability alongside business and economics, after one term to focus on the business full-time, once monthly sales reached around €1,000. The company, Poseidon Hair, turned over €272,000 last year and has since expanded to more than a dozen products, with the United States as its largest market, followed by Ireland, the UK and the rest of the EU.From €500 school project to €272,000 businessAccording to the Irish Times, Hefferon's path to entrepreneurship wasn't entirely straightforward. After leaving school, he enrolled at UCD to study sustainability alongside business and economics, but university life never quite clicked. By the end of his first term, sales of the sea spray were already ticking along at around €1,000 a month, and he decided to leave his course behind and commit to Poseidon full-time. As he put it himself, "I quickly discovered I was better at sales than studying."Hefferon lined up a subcontractor to manufacture the product and secured a fulfilment centre in Northern Ireland to manage distribution, and within months sales began climbing steadily. What started as an initial outlay of roughly €500, covering little more than basic packaging, has since grown into a business that turned over €272,000 in the past year alone, with the United States now its largest market, followed by Ireland, the UK and the rest of the EU.How Hefferon built Poseidon around hair-styling educationWhat sets Poseidon apart, according to Hefferon, isn't just the products themselves but the philosophy behind them. Rather than simply handing customers a jar or bottle and leaving them to work things out, he built the brand around teaching people how to actually use it. The idea grew directly out of conversations he was having in barbershops and online, where young men kept asking the same question: how to get more volume and movement in your hair, with no clear guidance available anywhere on the market.That gap led Hefferon to start filming tutorials that broke styling techniques down step by step, then designing products specifically to match what he was teaching. The range has since expanded well beyond the original spray to include a grooming clay, texture powder, moulding cream, hairspray, shampoo and conditioner, with further additions planned for 2026. While the core customer base sits between 16 and 24 years old, the appeal has stretched beyond that age group.How social media helped Poseidon reach customersToday, Poseidon remains a lean operation, run largely by Hefferon himself from Dublin, with just one part-time marketing professional helping to manage social media and email campaigns. TikTok and Instagram continue to serve as the company's main route to customers, and Hefferon keeps up a steady rhythm of daily videos and weekly styling tutorials, along with directly answering customer questions, an approach he intends to keep going for as long as he can manage it.Hefferon is pursuing a €150,000 funding round that would allow him to hire a chief marketing officer, ramp up production and widen the company's sales channels, including a push into pharmacies and expanded retail listings beyond its current presence on Amazon and in various barber shops. He credits the New Frontiers programme at TU Tallaght, along with mentoring from the Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown local enterprise office, with sharpening his understanding of his own business, though he readily admits that scaling a proven concept remains the hardest part of the journey, and the reason he's now taking an online course to build his e-commerce.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Italy endures hottest summer since records began
articles.summary: Italy recorded its hottest summer since 1950 this year, with the average temperature reaching 24. 3 degrees Celsius, the country's National Research Council...
articles.body:
Italy recorded its hottest summer since 1950 this year, with the average temperature reaching 24.3 degrees Celsius, the country's National Research Council (CNR) said on Monday.

August was particularly hot, with an average temperature of 25.6 degrees, according to data from the CNR's Institute for Bioeconomy. The figures are based on readings taken two metres above ground.

"The average temperature of 25.6 degrees measured in August 2026 exceeds the previous records of 24.6 degrees in 2024 and 24 degrees in August 2017," the CNR's Lorenzo Arcidiaco said.

Arcidiaco said the data also indicated that 2026 could become Italy's hottest year overall since records began in 1950.

Italy experienced several heatwaves over the summer, with temperatures soaring in major cities. The Health Ministry repeatedly issued its highest-level red heat alerts, warning of health risks even for healthy people exposed to the extreme conditions.

High temperatures combined with relatively high humidity made conditions particularly uncomfortable outdoors.

The CNR is Italy's largest public research institution.
